To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV infection of alveolar macro phages (AM) is facilitated by increased expression of FcgR1 and CR1 on these cells.
The expression of CR1 and CD64 by alveolar (lung) macrophages is increased in HIV+ patients.
the expression of CR1 and of FcγR1 on alveolarmacrophages from subjects with HIV infection increases as the disease advances.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the lung in the pathogenesis of AIDS.
the role of alveolar macrophase in the development of lung disease in HIV+ patients, and in particular, with the role of these cells in the development of interstitial pneumonia and Kaposi's sarcoma.
the study of the expression of receptors for the complement and Fc region of Ig on human alveolar macrophae (AM) during HIV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the expression of CR1 and/or FcγRI on AM is increased during the early stages of HIV infection and is progressive with disease progression.

HIV infection is associated with a progressive increase in expression of CR1 and, in particular, FcγRI by alveolar macropages, and that this increase is associated with a decline in peripheral CD4 count.
the expression of CR1 and/or FcγRI on alveolar monocytes/macrophages is increased in patients with HIV infection, and is associated with a decline in peripheral CD4 count.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the increased expression of FcgammaR on AM may be an important factor in facilitating HIV infection of AM and the subsequent progression of disease in these patients.
HIV disease progression is associated with increased FcγRI, but not CR3, expression by AM.
the increase in expression of Fc and complement receptors is an early event in the pathogenesis of HIV infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the increased expression of CR1 and especially FcγRI by AM during HIV infection could facilitate the uptake of immune complexes and viral particles, thereby increasing the potential for viral infection of these important cells.
HIV infection of the lung is associated with increased binding of immune complexes to the alveolar macro phages, and this may be a mechanism for viral infection of these macrophages.
the expression of receptors for FcγRI is significantly increased in HIV+ subjects.
